prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and the identification and synthesis of its active form, which made incretin-based therapy of type 2 diabetes and obesity possible

statement.case_for: I keep B033 as the sole prize part, and I reached that again from the first-round exchange, not from the six identical openings. The chain from incretin physiology (Holst), through proglucagon-derived peptide and receptor biology (Drucker), to identification and synthesis of the active truncated peptide (Mojsov) is original, mechanistically clear and mature, with large independent outcome trials in diabetes, obesity, and cardiovascular and renal disease. The chair asks whether the achievement is physiology or drug development. I say physiology: the discovery that gut-derived GLP-1(7-36) is the active, glucose-dependent incretin is what made every later molecule conceivable, and the citation can acknowledge the therapies without crediting the engineering. A two-part prize does not look justified to me. Adding a second part would cut the GLP-1 credit below three names and break the chain I find most convincing, and no other shortlisted candidate is strong enough in my judgement to accept that cost.
statement.case_against: The credit questions are real and round 1 did not remove them. Mojsov's priority for the active peptide against Habener and colleagues cannot be settled from the supplied material, and I rely partly on recalled priority histories. Knudsen's medicinal chemistry produced the long-acting agonists that patients actually receive, so a physiology trio can be read as honouring the hormone and not the medicine. If the committee concludes that the clinical impact lies mainly in the engineered drugs, my preferred trio becomes hard to defend. I also keep my earlier concern that public prominence of incretin therapy should not stand in for scientific judgment. I record Knudsen's exclusion as a deliberate choice forced by the physiology framing and the three-person cap, not as a judgment about the quality of her work.

responses.point: Perlmann argues that giving Knudsen the third slot would turn the prize into a drug-development award, while keeping her as the point to revisit if Mojsov's priority cannot be defended, and that rewarding translation is not alien to the prize.
responses.response: I agree that replacing Mojsov with Knudsen would change the citation from discovery to development, and I want any such change made explicitly. I also accept your qualification that translation is not foreign to this prize when it rests on a discovery. My answer is that the discovery here is complete inside the trio, so the prize does not need to reach the drug to be anchored in a real medical result. I would revisit Knudsen only if the record shows Mojsov's contribution was not distinct. From the nomination text I cannot show that, so I keep Mojsov.

responses.point: Sandberg says the Mojsov question should be checked against the record before the final ballot and not used as grounds to drop her, and that a prize in the cytokine area would force a harder comparison of cytokine claims than the ballots resolve.
responses.response: I accept the first point and will treat the Mojsov question as an open uncertainty, not as a reason to remove her: identification and synthesis of the active peptide changed what could be tested in humans, and Holst and Drucker's work rests on that. On B051 you are right that TNF biology by Cerami, Vilcek, Kollias and others lies outside the pair. I take that as a real weakness and I have not changed my view that Feldmann and Maini remain the cleanest two-person immunology configuration. But it is a reason to rank B051 as an alternative, not as a lead, and I now place it behind B033 more clearly than I did in round 1.

responses.point: Linnarsson says Eshhar's chimeric receptor is the invention and that the missing credit weakens B026 more than the chair indicated, and that B051's cytokine concept rests on TNF biology by uncredited people.
responses.response: I take the Eshhar point seriously and it changes how I hold B026. I would credit only June and Sadelain, not Rosenberg as in my opening, because Rosenberg's adoptive cell transfer and TIL work is a distinct line. Even then I would want the citation to say honestly that it recognises the design and clinical proof of engineered T cells and not the first chimeric receptor concept. On B051 I concede the attribution gap you describe. Where I differ is that I see the Feldmann and Maini contribution as the clinical demonstration that a single cytokine drives chronic inflammation, which is a defined, creditable step, even if the biology preceded it.

responses.point: The chair asks whether the Mojsov versus Habener question can be settled and, if not, whether Mojsov stays in the trio and on what stated basis.
responses.response: It cannot be settled from the supplied record, so I name the basis. Mojsov stays because her identification and synthesis of the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide is separable from the cloning and proglucagon work by others, and the citation uses that wording. If Habener's claim were judged equal and could not be fitted in three names, I would want that stated as an acknowledged limit of the cap and not hidden. I would not solve it by dropping the active-peptide element, since that would remove the link between physiology and therapy.

responses.point: El Manira ranks optogenetics lower because any trio drops Bamberg, Boyden or Miesenböck, and says a contested exclusion of credited people is a cost GLP-1 and TNF blockade do not carry to the same degree.
responses.response: I agree with your cost argument and it supports my decision to keep B007 off my alternatives. B033 carries one exclusion and B051 none among its credited pair, whereas B007 forces three. It also fits your point that Knudsen should be revisited only if Mojsov fails. I would add that the same logic argues against a two-part prize this year, because the cap would impose a second set of exclusions in the GLP-1 part.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's contribution to the active GLP-1 peptide is distinct enough from Habener and colleagues to credit, which the supplied evidence does not settle and which I partly judge from memory.
Whether the committee regards the achievement as the physiology or the drug development, since that decides whether Knudsen belongs in the trio.
Whether B026 can be framed honestly without Eshhar's chimeric receptor concept if GLP-1 does not hold.
Whether B051 allocation to Feldmann and Maini survives a check against earlier TNF work by Cerami, Vilcek, Kollias and others.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with B033. B051 (TNF blockade) lies in my clinical field of rheumatology. My profile records co-authors including Vijay Kuchroo and Sven-Erik Sonesson, and a group-leader affiliation at Bergen, and documents no link to Feldmann, Maini, June, Sadelain, Rosenberg or any credited name on B033. I infer no personal tie from shared field or institution. Disclosure unchanged from round 1.
